content.title: Comparing Mathematical Models
content.overview: This lesson focuses on evaluating and comparing different mathematical representations—such as equations, tables, or graphs—to determine which model produces a larger or different output for a specific input value.
learning_objectives: Identify the specific input value required for comparison.
Evaluate multiple models (linear, exponential, or tabular) at the same input point.
Compare numeric outputs using consistent units to determine the larger value.

sections.title: Recognizing Comparison Tasks
sections.content: On the ACT, you may be presented with two different models describing the same phenomenon (e.g., population growth, cost over time, or distance). One might be an equation, while the other is a table or a graph. The task is to determine which model yields a higher value at a specific point in time or for a specific quantity. The 'trigger' for this skill is any question asking which model is 'greater,' 'larger,' or 'more' at a given input $x$ or $t$.

sections.title: The Direct-Value Comparison Strategy
sections.content:
To compare models effectively, follow these steps: 1. Identify the target input value. 2. Substitute that exact value into every model provided. 3. Calculate the output for each. If the calculation is complex, use estimation or your calculator to find a decimal approximation. 4. Ensure all outputs are in the same units (e.g., converting minutes to hours if necessary) before making the final comparison.

![A flowchart showing the steps to compare two mathematical models: Identify Input, Substitute into Models, Compute Outputs, and Compare Values.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/c1765e13-e497-4a7c-8d7b-b5861577c2bf-1786506342058-785.webp)

sections.title: Linear vs. Exponential Growth
sections.content: A common comparison involves a linear model (additive change) and an exponential model (multiplicative change). Linear models like $y = mx + b$ grow by a constant amount each step. Exponential models like $y = a(b)^x$ grow by a percentage or factor. Even if a linear model starts higher, an exponential model with a growth factor greater than 1 will eventually surpass it. Always calculate the specific point requested rather than assuming based on the starting values.

worked_examples.question: Two models estimate a bacteria population $P$ after $t$ hours. Model A: $P(t) = 120(1.2)^t$. Model B: $P(t) = 100 + 20t$. Which model predicts a larger population at $t = 10$?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the input, which is $t = 10$. Step 2: Evaluate Model A. $P(10) = 120(1.2)^{10}$. Using a calculator, $1.2^{10} \approx 6.19$. So, $120 \times 6.19 \approx 743$. Step 3: Evaluate Model B. $P(10) = 100 + 20(10) = 100 + 200 = 300$. Step 4: Compare the results. Since $743 > 300$, Model A predicts a significantly larger population.

common_mistakes: Confusing the rate of change with the total output value.
Assuming a model is 'larger' overall just because its starting value (y-intercept) is higher.
Failing to use the same input value for both models.
Mistaking exponential growth (multiplication) for linear growth (addition).
exam_tips: If one model is a graph, locate the input on the x-axis and find the corresponding y-value visually to compare with your calculated value.
Watch for unit mismatches; if Model A uses seconds and Model B uses minutes, convert them to match before comparing.
Use the 'Table' function on your graphing calculator to quickly compare values across multiple inputs if the question asks for a range.
content.recap: To compare models, substitute the same input into each representation, calculate the outputs, and identify which result is numerically greater. Do not rely on growth descriptions alone; always perform the substitution.

knowledge_claims.content: To compare two models at a specific point, substitute the same input value into both representations and calculate the resulting outputs.
A comparison task is triggered when a question asks which of two models yields a larger or different value for a given variable.
Before comparing numeric outputs from different models, verify that all values are expressed in consistent units.
Linear models represent constant additive change, whereas exponential models represent constant multiplicative change.
It is a mistake to assume a model with a higher y-intercept will always yield a larger output than a model with a lower y-intercept.
In the exponential model $P(t) = 120(1.2)^t$, the value $1.2$ represents a 20% growth rate per unit of time, not an addition of 1.2 units.
When comparing an equation to a graph, find the y-value on the graph at the specified x-coordinate to compare it to the equation's calculated result.
An exponential growth model with a base greater than 1 will eventually exceed any linear growth model, regardless of initial values.
If exact arithmetic is time-consuming during a comparison, use estimation or a calculator to find decimal approximations of the outputs.
Confusing the rate of change (slope) with the actual output value (y-value) at a specific point is a common error in modeling questions.
The input variable is the independent value (often $x$ or $t$) that is plugged into a model to determine the output (often $y$ or $P$).
Always confirm that the same input value was used for both models before selecting an answer choice.

items.stem:
Practice form 1.
Two models fit the same data. Which comparison is most useful?
A) Compare prediction error and whether each model's assumptions are reasonable.
B) Choose the model with the longer equation only.
C) Choose at random without checking data.
D) Use the model with more letters regardless of fit.

options.A: Compare prediction error and whether each model's assumptions are reasonable.
options.B: Choose the model with the longer equation only.
options.C: Choose at random without checking data.
options.D: Use the model with more letters regardless of fit.

items.explanation: Model comparison should consider fit and assumptions.

videoLesson.title: Compare Model Outputs At A Given Input
videoLesson.description: Recognize which model yields the larger numeric output for a specified input variable. Substitute the input into each model, compute outputs with consistent units, and compare values to decide.
